family: ternary counter on runs of alternating cells
summary: An exact ternary counter, least significant digit at the left end, whose digits are pairs of long runs of alternating cells read mod 4; every trip of the head adds one, and the increment is proved in Lean for every carry depth. Open: the transfers that happen when a shrinking run runs out, and the right end.
title: What is known about 1RB0RA_1LC0RE_0LD0LB_1LA1LF_1RA0LF_1LC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RA_1LC0RE_0LD0LB_1LA1LF_1RA0LF_1LC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is an exact ternary counter: its digits are pairs of runs of alternating cells, valued by their lengths mod 4, and each trip of the head adds one. That increment is proved in Lean (kernel) for every carry depth, and it covers 99.86% of the trips in the first 3·1012 steps. The counter keeps shrinking one run of each digit; when such a run runs out, a transfer moves a long run to the right end of the tape. Transfers and the right end are not yet described by rules, so non-halting is not proved.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 76,685 cells have been visited and 38,338 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.554). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.389).

claims.title: Sweep moves
claims.text: L A>(0101)^n R → L (1010)^n A> R (4n steps: going right A flips the phase of a block), L (01)^n B>0 R → L B>0 (01)^n R and L (10)^n C>1 R → L C>1 (10)^n R (2n steps: going left blocks are crossed unchanged), for every n, L, R.

claims.title: The pieces of a trip
claims.text: Eight rules for all run lengths and every surrounding tape: digit 0 going from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 2 (whole trips), the carry leaving digit 0, the carry passing a digit at 2 (a bounce), the carry stopping at a digit at 1 or at 0, and going home over a passed digit and over digit 0, with exact step counts.

claims.title: The increment, for every carry depth
claims.text: By induction over the list of digits a carry passes: from the start of a trip with digit 0 at 2, any number of digits at 2, then a digit at 1 (or at 0), the machine reaches the start of the next trip with the exact tape and step count stated. With inc0 and inc1 this is every kind of trip while the runs involved are long enough (r0 ≥ 7, r1 ≥ 5, a passed digit x ≥ 9, y ≥ 5, the stopping digit x ≥ 4, y ≥ 6 or x ≥ 6, y ≥ 7).

claims.title: The run-length table of a trip
claims.text: Read off the Lean statements: digit 0 changes (r0, r1) by (+2, +3) and takes one cell from x1, by (+5, −1), or by (+1, +2) when it carries; a passed digit changes by (−2, +2), a digit going from 1 to 2 by (+2, −1), from 0 to 1 by (−1, +3) and takes one cell from the next digit. Checked by expanding the statements for 2,000 random parameter choices.

claims.title: An exact fast simulator
claims.text: py/rsim.py runs the machine on a run-length tape with the three proved sweep moves; it agrees with a plain cell simulator on the step of every one of the 17,669 trip starts in the first 4·109 steps.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>14</sup> steps
claims.text: py/rsim.py runs 1014 steps without a halt (3,153,668 trips).

claims.title: 99.86% of trips are the proved kinds
claims.text: Of the 726,270 trips in the first 3·10<sup>12</sup> steps, 725,254 have one of the four proved shapes with the runs long enough. Of the other 1,016, the carry reaches the right end in 98, a run is too short in 269, and a digit has residues outside the table in 648 (and one is the first trip). They come, as far as we have looked, with transfers (a run x<sub>k</sub> has run out and the run y<sub>k−1</sub> is shuttled, two cells at a time, to the right end of the tape, after which the digits past it are paired anew) or with the right end, where new digits are made from short runs.

claims.title: How close it comes to halting
claims.text: The machine halts exactly when D reads a 1 whose left neighbour is a 1. Of the 6,032,756 times D read a 1 in the first 3·10<sup>12</sup> steps, the alternating stretch ending at D's cell had length 2 158 times and length 3 17 times (a halt needs length 1); those we looked at were near the right end or in transfers.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The increment is proved; transfers and the right end are only observed. A halt could only come from them.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. This machine counts in base 3, least significant digit at the left end. Its tape is a row of long runs of alternating cells; each pair of neighbouring runs is a digit, valued by the run lengths mod 4, and every trip of the head from the left end and back adds one. The increment is proved; what happens when a shrinking run runs out is not.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.554). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.389).
After 109 steps the tape spans 76,685 cells (39,628 left of the start, 15,538 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Runs of alternating cells
html: Cut the tape into maximal runs of alternating cells, 0101… or 1010…. Two neighbouring runs meet at a doubled cell, 00 or 11, so the list of run lengths says everything (the first run starts with 0). At the start of a trip (A at the left end) the runs are, at step 10,000,025,550:
Name them r0 r1 | x1 y1 | x2 y2 | …: digit 0 is (r0, r1), digit k is (xk, yk).

sections.heading: A counter in base 3
html: A digit's value is read from its two run lengths mod 4:

valuedigit 0 (r0, r1) mod 4digit k (x, y) mod 4
0(0, 3)(2, 3)
1(2, 2)(0, 2)
2(3, 1)(1, 1)
(After digit k changes, xk can be one cell longer than this reading, until digit k−1 next goes from 0 to 1 and takes that cell.) Each trip adds one, and the runs change by a few cells:

digitchangeruns
00 → 1r0 + 2, r1 + 3, x1 − 1
01 → 2r0 + 5, r1 − 1
02 → 0, carryr0 + 1, r1 + 2
k2 → 0, carryx − 2, y + 2
k1 → 2x + 2, y − 1
k0 → 1x − 1, y + 3, next x − 1

Going right, A flips every cell it passes. A carry is a bounce: B meets the 00 at the start of xk, runs back over yk−1, turns, and goes on through digit k. Where the carry stops the head turns and goes home, B and C carrying the pattern one cell along; the left end grows by 4 cells per trip.
All of this is proved in Lean, for all run lengths and for every carry depth at once (an induction over the digits the carry passes): trip_stop1, trip_stop0, inc0, inc1 in lean/Counter.lean.

sections.eyebrow: Why it is not a proof yet
sections.heading: Runs that run out
html: Over one cycle of digit k (3k+1 trips) xk loses 4 cells and yk gains 4, so every xk eventually runs out. Then the next carry does not bounce through: the head shuttles between the end of yk−1 and the right end of the tape, moving yk−1 two cells at a time to the far right (a transfer; these are the long pauses of the run and the reason the right side grows). Afterwards the digits past it are paired anew and counting goes on. For example at step 39,282 the runs 187 97 2 31 25 7 7 become 186 43 27 5 13 177. New digits are made at the right end from short runs.
In the first 3·1012 steps 99.86% of the 726,270 trips are the proved kinds; the rest come with transfers or the right end, which are only observed.

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The only halting transition is F on a 1. F comes from E (on a cell B has just made 0, so F reads that 0) or from D, and D only from C on a 0. So the machine halts exactly when D reads a 1 whose left neighbour is also a 1. In the proved trips that never happens. In the first 3·1012 steps D read a 1 about six million times; the alternating stretch ending at D's cell was 2 cells long 158 times and 3 cells long 17 times (a halt needs 1), in the cases we looked at near the right end or in a transfer.
So a halt, if any, would come from a transfer or from the right end. The exact simulator finds none in 1014 steps.
